measurement.happened:
This week in DR Congo was dominated by two intertwined crises: a rapidly worsening Ebola outbreak and the ongoing military and diplomatic standoff with Rwanda over the M23 rebellion, all played out against the backdrop of the Francophonie summit in Cambodia.

THE EBOLA OUTBREAK (supported by nearly every source): The single biggest story of the week was the Ebola epidemic, now in its sixth month and clearly accelerating. The UN reported 5,500 deaths (Reuters, 11-18), while Deutsche Welle reported the caseload had just crossed 6,000 (11-21). Africa CDC declared the outbreak 'still not under control' (Reuters 11-16, Al Jazeera 11-15, AP 11-15). Reuters noted the virus is killing at a 'record pace' (11-17) and that scientists are still learning about this particular rare strain (11-20). Handicap International, cited by AFP (11-21) and TV5Monde (11-20), identified geography, ongoing violence, and community distrust as the three main obstacles to containment. Bloomberg (11-16) framed the crisis as being fueled by conflict and hunger, making it a compound emergency. The economic ripple effects were already visible: Barrick Gold furloughed some personnel at its Congo mines over Ebola concerns (Reuters, 11-17). A genuinely important development is that the WHO announced strain-specific Ebola vaccine trials are set to begin in DR Congo 'next week' (AFP, 11-17), which is a concrete near-term event. TV5Monde ran a video piece on the 'urgency' of containing the epidemic (11-16) and another on the 5,500+ dead (11-15).

RWANDA-DR CONGO TENSIONS AND M23 (supported by BBC, Al Jazeera, DW, TV5Monde, Reuters): The military conflict in the east, centered on the M23 rebel group, remained a major thread. BBC ran a dedicated M23 piece (11-18) and reported that the OIF (Operation of the Force, the regional military mechanism) is expected to come online within about two months (11-15). Al Jazeera reported that rival peace efforts have failed to halt violence in the east (11-18) and asked what is holding up the Washington-brokered peace process between Rwanda and DRC (11-18). Reuters noted that former Congo-based fighters are being retrained in Rwanda, swapping guns for new skills (11-20), suggesting both sides are preparing for a longer fight. DW described the M23 conflict as dividing the Francophone world (11-15). TV5Monde carried a video titled 'Humor as a weapon against war' (11-19), a small cultural note showing how the conflict permeates daily life.

THE FRANCOPHONIE SUMMIT (supported by AFP, DW, TV5Monde, Al Jazeera): The Francophone summit opened in Cambodia (11-15) and immediately became a stage for the DRC-Rwanda clash. AFP reported the summit 'opens with DR Congo, Rwandan clash' (11-15). DW noted Macron urged 'unity' and 'consensus' in the face of the tensions (11-15). TV5Monde ran multiple pieces on the summit and the DRC-Rwanda rift (11-15). DW also noted that DRC threatened to quit the Francophonie organization (11-15). Al Jazeera covered the summit opening amid the rift (11-15). This was a diplomatic flashpoint that amplified the bilateral conflict into a multilateral one.

US-DR CONGO MINERAL DEAL AND THE 'RESOURCES CURSE' (supported by BBC, TV5Monde, DW): BBC ran a feature asking whether a US-backed mineral highway can bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo (11-18). TV5Monde reported on the status of the bilateral US-DRC agreement on copper, cobalt, tin, and dams, now nearly a year after signing (11-18), and separately noted that US Democrats want to investigate Trump's mineral agreements in Africa, including with DRC, Zambia, and Kenya (11-19). DW published a piece on DRC's 'resources curse' (11-21), framing the country's vast mineral wealth as a source of both power and exploitation. This cluster of stories shows the mineral deal is a live political issue both in Kinshasa and in Washington.

SMALLER DOMESTIC NOTES (TV5Monde): Boat operators in wood went on strike (11-18). R&B star Héritier Wata announced he is 'already in the studio' with Fally Ipupa to record their long-awaited collaboration (11-18), a light cultural moment amid the crisis. These are minor but show the country's everyday life continuing.
measurement.expected:
EBOLA OUTBREAK (confidence: almost certain the outbreak remains the top story; probable that caseload crosses 7,000 and deaths pass 6,000): The WHO's announcement that strain-specific vaccine trials begin 'next week' (AFP, 11-17) is the most concrete near-term event to watch. Expect the first trial sites to be activated in the Kivu or South Kivu region, with WHO and Africa CDC issuing briefings on enrollment. The outbreak is still accelerating, so expect the death toll to climb past 6,000 and the caseload past 7,000 by the end of the following week, consistent with the 'record pace' Reuters described. Barrick and other mining operators may announce further furloughs or safety protocols as the virus spreads toward industrial zones. Handicap International's warnings about geography, violence, and distrust suggest that containment in remote eastern areas will remain weak, and we may see a new cluster reported in a previously unaffected district. The UN will likely issue another appeal for funding or personnel. Probability of a dramatic new twist, such as a second strain being confirmed or the virus reaching a major city like Goma or Bukavu: possible but not the base case.

RWANDA-DR CONGO / M23 (confidence: probable that violence continues in the east; possible that OIF planning accelerates): The BBC report that the OIF is expected within two months means the next week will likely see more diplomatic shuffling and troop-mobilization announcements from the East African Community or SADC. Al Jazeera's reporting that rival peace efforts have 'failed to halt violence' suggests the Washington process is stuck, and we should expect more frustrated statements from both Kinshasa and Kigali. The retraining of ex-Congo fighters in Rwanda (Reuters, 11-20) hints at continued military preparation. A localized escalation or a new M23 offensive in the North Kivu or South Kivu corridor is probable. A full-scale ceasefire or a major diplomatic breakthrough this week: unlikely.

FRANCOPHONIE AFTERMATH (confidence: probable that diplomatic spillover continues): The summit just concluded, so the next week will likely bring formal communiqués, follow-up statements, and possibly a DRC decision on whether to stay in or exit the Francophonie (the threat DW reported on 11-15). Expect more rhetoric from both sides and possibly a joint statement or a walkout by one party at a smaller follow-up meeting. A formal DRC withdrawal from the organization this week: possible but would be a dramatic step; more likely they issue a strong statement first.

US MINERAL DEAL / DOMESTIC POLITICS (confidence: possible that Democratic investigation news breaks; probable that the deal remains a talking point): TV5Monde's report that Democrats want to investigate Trump's African mineral agreements (11-19) suggests that in the next week we may see a formal inquiry announcement, a letter to the White House, or Congressional hearings scheduled. The BBC's mineral-highway feature (11-18) and DW's 'resources curse' piece (11-21) indicate growing public and media scrutiny of the deal's benefits for Congolese citizens. Expect Kinshasa to respond publicly, either defending the deal or calling for renegotiation. A formal renegotiation or a new bilateral meeting this week: possible but not the base case.

DOMESTIC LIFE (confidence: probable that the boat strike and other labor actions continue or resolve quietly; the Wata-Ipupa studio news will generate cultural buzz): The wood-boat operators' strike (TV5Monde, 11-18) may see a resolution or a small escalation. The Wata-Ipupa collaboration announcement will dominate Congolese social media and entertainment coverage. These are low-stakes but will keep the domestic news cycle alive.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES (possible but not the base case): a new Ebola cluster in a previously unaffected province; a sudden M23 offensive that captures a key town; a formal DRC withdrawal from the Francophonie; a US Congressional resolution on the mineral deal; a major mining company suspending operations entirely; a DRC presidential visit to Kigali or vice versa.

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON: a full Ebola containment declaration; a signed DRC-Rwanda peace treaty; a US-DRC mineral deal renegotiation or cancellation; a new presidential election or cabinet reshuffle; a major natural disaster (flood, earthquake); a coup or military takeover; the Wata-Ipupa song being released and topping charts this week; a new international summit specifically on DRC.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the Ebola outbreak remains the single most prominent story but its framing shifted. In the first week the emphasis was on raw numbers climbing past 11,000 cases and 5,387 deaths, with MSF and the CDC issuing alarms. By the second week the numbers are still grim—5,500 deaths per the UN, a caseload that Deutsche Welle puts at 6,000—and the narrative has moved from 'the numbers are shocking' to 'here is why we cannot stop it.' Handicap International's triad of geography, violence, and community distrust, Bloomberg's framing of the crisis as fueled by conflict and hunger, and the WHO's announcement of strain-specific vaccine trials all signal a shift from shock to operational analysis. The outbreak did not accelerate in the way the first week's headlines implied, but it did not slow down either; it has become the permanent backdrop against which everything else is measured. The military thread grew and sharpened. In the first photograph the eastern conflict was a multi-front blur: ADF killing civilians, FRN rebels, 66 soldiers sentenced to death, M23 mentioned in passing. By the second photograph M23 and the Rwanda dimension have consolidated into the central military story, with the regional OIF mechanism expected to activate within two months, a Washington-brokered peace process under scrutiny, and former Congo-based fighters being retrained in Rwanda. The ADF and the death sentences faded from the headlines. The Francophonie summit moved from a background diplomatic squabble over the OIF leadership to a live, on-camera clash in Cambodia, with DR Congo explicitly threatening to quit the organization. That is a step up in intensity. A new theme appeared that was absent from the first photograph: the US-DRC mineral deal and the broader 'resources curse.' BBC, TV5Monde, and DW all ran pieces on the copper-cobalt-tin-dam agreement, US Democrats' push to investigate Trump's African mineral pacts, and the structural question of whether mineral wealth is a blessing or a trap. This is a genuinely new political-economic thread. The constitutional and internal-politics thread shrank noticeably. The referendum law, the Kabila street renaming, the Lambert Mende defection, and the Étienne Tshisekedi national-hero bid were all prominent in the first photograph and are largely silent in the second. The lighter items rotated: the CAN qualifiers and the AI-coders story vanished, replaced by a boat-operators' strike and the Héritier Wata–Fally Ipupa studio announcement. Cholera, mentioned in the first week, does not reappear. The tin-deal talks are gone, though the Barrick furlough persists as a recurring economic footnote.
delta.wind: On Ebola, the expectation was broadly correct. The outbreak stayed dominant, the Africa CDC and other bodies kept saying it was not under control, the Barrick furlough generated follow-up, and there was no sudden containment declaration. What came in a different form: the narrative moved from 'the numbers are terrifying' to 'here are the structural reasons it will not end soon,' and the WHO vaccine-trial announcement added a concrete near-term event that was not on the expectation list. The expectation that case and death numbers would keep climbing at a steep rate was only partially borne out; the death toll ticked up modestly from 5,387 to 5,500, and the caseload figure in the second photograph (6,000 per DW) is actually lower than the 11,000 cited in the first, suggesting either a reporting discrepancy, a change in what is being counted, or a deceleration that the 'still not under control' language papers over. On the constitutional and political thread, the expectation was that the referendum law and third-term debate would keep generating headlines. In reality that thread shrank rather than expanded. The law was signed in the first week, and by the second week the headlines had moved on to the summit, the mineral deal, and the military. The Kabila street renaming, the Lambert Mende realignment, and the national-hero controversy all faded. The expectation of opposition rallies or a constitutional crisis did not materialize, which was the 'unlikely' scenario, but the thread simply lost momentum rather than exploding. On the eastern conflict, the expectation of more ADF or FRN attacks was partially right in the sense that violence continued, but the focus shifted to M23 and the Rwanda dimension, which the expectation had flagged as a 'possible' resurfacing. The M23 thread grew into the central military story, which was more than the expectation projected. The OIF timeline and the retraining of ex-fighters in Rwanda were not in the expectation list at all. On the Francophonie summit, the expectation of further diplomatic statements was confirmed, and the DRC threat to quit the organization was a step beyond what was anticipated. The 'unlikely' scenario of a full rupture did not happen. The CAN qualifier results and the national-hero opinion pieces, expected as near-certain lighter news, did not appear in the second photograph, replaced by the boat strike and the Wata-Ipupa story. The biggest miss was the US mineral deal and the 'resources curse' framing, which was not on the expectation list at all but became a significant cluster of reporting. This suggests that for DR Congo, the expectation model tends to over-weight internal political maneuvering and under-weight the external economic and military dimensions, particularly the US-Rwanda-DRC triangle and the way mineral politics now intersects with every other story. The model also tends to assume that a signed law will generate a sustained news cycle, when in practice Kinshasa's political stories have a short half-life unless they are tied to a visible street-level event.
delta.driver: The force pushing DR Congo from the first photograph to the second is the convergence of a health emergency and a military conflict in a country whose economy, governance, and international standing all hinge on its minerals. Ebola is not just a disease; it is being made worse by the violence in the east, the geography of the affected regions, and the community distrust that war has bred, while simultaneously weakening the very populations and health systems that the M23 conflict depends on. The Rwanda-DRC standoff, which in the first week was one thread among several, has consolidated into the dominant military narrative because both sides are now preparing for a longer fight—retraining fighters, planning the OIF deployment, and testing each other at the Francophonie summit. The US mineral deal adds a third axis: Washington is now a direct economic and political stakeholder in Kinshasa's resource strategy, which means every Ebola-related furlough at a Barrick mine, every 'resources curse' op-ed, and every Democratic congressional inquiry is pulling the country's story in a new direction. In short, the country is being compressed from three sides at once—health from the south and east, military pressure from the east, and economic-political leverage from the west and the east—and the internal political threads (the referendum, the street renaming, the cabinet shuffle) are being squeezed into the margins because the population and the press are focused on survival, not succession.

crystal.eli5:
DR Congo is dealing with a really bad Ebola outbreak that has been going on for about six months. More than 5,500 people have died, and the virus is a rare strain that scientists are still learning about. The big news for next week is that a new vaccine trial specifically for this strain is starting. That is a small step toward a cure, but the outbreak is not slowing down, and the places where it is hitting hardest are also where the war in the east is happening, which makes it harder to treat people and keep them safe.

At the same time, DR Congo and its neighbor Rwanda are still stuck in a tense standoff over a rebel group called M23. They are not at full-scale war right now, but they are both preparing for a longer fight. A regional peacekeeping force is supposed to start working in about two months, so next week is more about diplomacy and small skirmishes than a big battle. The two countries also got into a public argument at a French-language summit in Cambodia, and DR Congo even threatened to quit the whole organization, though that is more of a negotiating move than something that will actually happen next week.

A new thread that has been growing is the deal between the US and DR Congo about copper, cobalt, and other minerals. US politicians who are not in the president's party want to look into whether the deal is fair, and a big mining company already paused some work because of Ebola. So the health crisis, the war, and the money from minerals are all starting to tangle together in ways that make every story affect every other story. The government at home is trying to manage all of this, but the internal political fights from a few weeks ago have mostly quieted down because everyone is focused on the bigger emergencies.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A correctly identified Ebola as the dominant story and nailed the death toll at 5,500, which matched the UN figure reported by Reuters. It also correctly predicted the Barrick Gold furlough, the Africa CDC/WHO warnings about the outbreak being out of control, and the DRC-Rwanda diplomatic sparring around the Francophonie summit. Its prediction that the Francophonie clash would produce statements and diplomatic notes was broadly right, as the DRC threatened to quit and Macron urged unity. However, A significantly overestimated the Ebola case count, predicting 12,000 to 13,000 when the actual figure was just past 6,000. A also overemphasized several threads that were not prominent this week: the parallel cholera epidemic (not a major headline), the killing of health workers by ADF specifically (M23 dominated rebel coverage), the 66 death sentences rippling through the army (not a major story), and the constitutional/symbolic campaign (street renamings, Tshisekedi as national hero, C64 opposition rally, Lambert Mende realignment). A's prediction of a Merck/Ervebo procurement update was close in spirit to the WHO's announcement of strain-specific vaccine trials, but the specific framing was off. A missed the US-DRC bilateral mineral agreement as a major political story, the US Democrats' push to investigate Trump's African mineral deals, the 'resources curse' framing, the OIF two-month timeline, and the retraining of former Congo fighters in Rwanda. A's overall picture was directionally correct on the big themes but over-specified on several sub-threads that did not materialize, and it got the scale of the Ebola caseload wrong by roughly a factor of two.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B also correctly identified Ebola as the dominant story and the DRC-Rwanda/M23 tension as a major thread. It correctly predicted that the outbreak would remain out of control, that case numbers would climb, and that the death toll would tick upward. Its prediction of diplomatic sparring from Kinshasa or Kigali was confirmed by the DRC threatening to quit the Francophonie. B correctly noted that M23 could resurface, which it did as a major thread. It also correctly identified the Barrick furlough and the OIF leadership question. However, B also overestimated the Ebola case count, predicting above 11,000 when the actual was around 6,000, though its error was less dramatic than A's. B did not over-predict the cholera epidemic, the ADF-specific violence, or the constitutional/symbolic campaign, all of which were not major stories this week. B missed the US-DRC mineral deal as a major political story (it mentioned 'tin-deal talks' in passing but not the broader bilateral agreement or the US political dimension), the WHO strain-specific vaccine trial announcement, the 'resources curse' framing, and the US Democrats' investigation push. B's list of 'less likely surprises' (power outage, cabinet reshuffle, cholera cluster, coup) all did not happen, which is fine since they were labeled unlikely. B's overall picture was more conservative and fewer of its specific predictions were contradicted by the actual week.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts got the two dominant themes right: Ebola as the overwhelming story and the DRC-Rwanda/M23/Francophonie diplomatic clash. Both correctly identified the Barrick furlough and the general trajectory of the outbreak. Both missed the US-DRC bilateral mineral agreement as a major political story and the WHO vaccine trial announcement, which were significant concrete developments. The key differences are in the sub-threads. Forecast A made more specific predictions that did not materialize: the parallel cholera epidemic as a major headline, ADF-specific violence (when M23 dominated), the 66 death sentences generating visible army reactions, street renamings, the C64 opposition rally, and the Tshisekedi national-hero debate. A also overestimated the Ebola case count by roughly a factor of two (12,000-13,000 vs. 6,000). Forecast B was more restrained, hedged more, and made fewer specific predictions that could be contradicted.
